evidence_items.claim: Mark's conflicts with particular Jewish leaders cannot authorize antisemitism, supersessionism, deicide accusations, collective Jewish guilt, or portraying Pharisees and Judaism as uniquely hypocritical, impure, or hard-hearted.
Mark preserves and translates several Semitic expressions, including Boanerges, Talitha koum, Corban, Ephphatha, Bartimaeus, Abba, Golgotha, and Eloi.

Mark's healing stories portray embodied need and restored participation, yet cure-centered reception can stigmatize disabled people and must not equate bodily difference with sin, weak faith, or spiritual failure.
The grammar and scope of Mark 7:19 remain disputed; readings range from an editorial declaration about all foods to an anatomical claim about digestion that does not repeal kashrut.
Mark narrates some disciples eating bread with common, unwashed hands before expanding into command, tradition, ingestion, and defilement.

evidence_items.claim: Mark's Sabbath, handwashing, purity, divorce, commandment, and temple disputes are intrajewish arguments in a Jewish scriptural world, not evidence that Judaism was uniquely legalistic.
Rome, Syria, Galilee, and other settings have been proposed, but no city or single ethnic audience can be established from the text.
The Syrophoenician woman answers Jesus' children-and-dogs saying and obtains her daughter's release; interpretations of testing, boundary, ethnicity, gender, and change remain disputed.
The operative setting is Hellenistic and Roman Judaism, not generic Ancient Near Eastern leadership.
Pharisaic positions in ancient sources concern Torah, ancestral tradition, providence, purity, resurrection, and communal practice within Jewish covenant life.

Pharisees are securely attested in Hasmonean and Roman-period sources. Their membership, organization, social reach, and relationship to later rabbis remain debated, and Gospel polemic cannot serve as a neutral institutional census.
Judea and Galilee from the Hasmonean period through 70 CE, with Josephus writing after the temple's destruction.
Readers of the Gospels and Acts encountering a named Jewish group through diverse narrative and historical lenses.
Josephus distinguishes Pharisees from Sadducees and Essenes; the Gospels narrate both disputes and shared assumptions; Acts identifies Paul with Pharisaic training and resurrection hope.
Workshop caves and production debris at Reina, approximately three kilometers from Nazareth, attest regional manufacture of soft-limestone vessels used in Jewish settlements.
The workshops show that stone vessels associated with purity practice were locally available, contextualizing John 2 and purity disputes without identifying the Cana jars or Mark's opponents.
Writing specialists served courts, temples, and administrations across the ancient world, but late Second Temple scribal roles require direct Jewish and Greco-Roman-period evidence.
Scribal learning centers on transmitted instruction, wise judgment, Torah interpretation, teaching, and communal responsibility, while biblical texts also criticize misuse of status and expertise.

The label scribe does not denote one unchanging profession. Royal and administrative scribes, Ezra's priestly-scribal commission, Ben Sira's learned ideal, and Gospel legal experts belong to different periods and institutions.
Israelite, Persian-period, Hellenistic, and Roman settings; the office must be dated passage by passage.
Readers distinguishing administrative, literary, priestly, and legal scribal roles across biblical periods.
Ezra and Ben Sira reflect priestly and learned forms of scribal identity; the Gospels and Acts often associate scribes with legal interpretation, Jerusalem leadership, and public debate.
4QMMT preserves disputed rulings, Galilean limestone workshops attest purity-oriented vessels, and Mishnah Yadayim later details hand purification.
